evidence.paraphrase: The narrator concludes from her own feelings that she is an experiment.
evidence.quote: I feel like an experiment, I feel exactly like an experiment; it would be impossible for a person to feel more like an experiment than I do, and so I am coming to feel convinced that that is what I AM--an experiment; just an experiment, and nothing more.

evidence.paraphrase: The world is depicted as newly created and nearly finished.
evidence.quote: this majestic new world is indeed a most noble and beautiful work.  And certainly marvelously near to being perfect, notwithstanding the shortness of the time.

evidence.paraphrase: The moon detaches and falls out of the sky, described as a loss.
evidence.quote: The moon got loose last night, and slid down and fell out of the scheme--a very great loss; it breaks my heart to think of it.

evidence.paraphrase: She attempts by trial to knock stars down, learning they are out of reach.
evidence.quote: When they first showed, last night, I tried to knock some down with a pole, but it didn't reach, which astonished me; then I tried clods till I was all tired out, but I never got one.

evidence.paraphrase: She reasons that stars are much farther away than they appear.
evidence.quote: You would be surprised to find how far off they are, for they do not look it.

evidence.paraphrase: She formulates a general axiom from experience with distances and thorns.
evidence.quote: I learned a lesson; also I made an axiom, all out of my own head--my very first one; THE SCRATCHED EXPERIMENT SHUNS THE THORN.

evidence.paraphrase: She observes and tracks the other creature to determine its purpose.
evidence.quote: I followed the other Experiment around, yesterday afternoon, at a distance, to see what it might be for, if I could.

evidence.paraphrase: She reacts with thrill to hearing another's speech for the first time.
evidence.quote: It gave me a thrill, for it was the first time I had ever heard speech, except my own.  I did not understand the words, but they seemed expressive.

evidence.paraphrase: She claims an immediate, inspired ability to name each animal.
evidence.quote: The minute I set eyes on an animal I know what it is.  I don't have to reflect a moment; the right name comes out instantly

evidence.paraphrase: She names fire by sudden inspiration despite never having encountered it.
evidence.quote: Suddenly the name of it occurred to me, though I had never heard of it before.  It was FIRE! I was as certain of it as a person could be of anything in the world.

evidence.paraphrase: She claims to have introduced fire, a new phenomenon, into the world.
evidence.quote: I had created something that didn't exist before; I had added a new thing to the world's uncountable properties

evidence.paraphrase: She names smoke on first sight of it.
evidence.quote: the blue spirit was towering up and stretching and rolling away like a cloud, and instantly I thought of the name of it--SMOKE!--though, upon my word, I had never heard of smoke before.

evidence.paraphrase: She reacts with joy and rapture to the sight of flames.
evidence.quote: I had to clap my hands and laugh and dance in my rapture, it was so new and strange and so wonderful and so beautiful!

evidence.paraphrase: Through fire she discovers the emotion of fear for the first time.
evidence.quote: the fire had revealed to me a new passion--quite new, and distinctly different from love, grief, and those others which I had already discovered--FEAR.  And it is horrible!

evidence.paraphrase: Adam contrasts his and Eve's opposite reactions to the brontosaurus.
evidence.quote: She wanted to domesticate it, I wanted to make it a present of the homestead and move out.

evidence.paraphrase: A living brontosaurus appears in their setting, mixing eras.
evidence.quote: When the mighty brontosaurus came striding into camp, she regarded it as an acquisition, I considered it a calamity

evidence.paraphrase: She articulates a method of proving things by experiment rather than conjecture.
evidence.quote: It is best to prove things by actual experiment; then you KNOW; whereas if you depend on guessing and supposing and conjecturing, you never get educated.

evidence.paraphrase: She reasons by cumulative evidence from experiments about floating.
evidence.quote: By experiment I know that wood swims, and dry leaves, and feathers, and plenty of other things; therefore by all that cumulative evidence you know that a rock will swim

evidence.paraphrase: She proposes an optical-illusion explanation for observed falling objects.
evidence.quote: Of course it DOESN'T come down, but why should it SEEM to? I suppose it is an optical illusion.

evidence.paraphrase: She generalizes from observing meteors that all stars can melt away.
evidence.quote: By watching, I know that the stars are not going to last. I have seen some of the best ones melt and run down the sky. Since one can melt, they can all melt

evidence.paraphrase: The Garden is now lost following the Fall, marking a changed state.
evidence.quote: When I look back, the Garden is a dream to me.  It was beautiful, surpassingly beautiful, enchantingly beautiful; and now it is lost, and I shall not see it any more.

evidence.paraphrase: The narrative jumps forward forty years in time.
evidence.quote: Forty Years Later

evidence.paraphrase: Her feelings are projected forward as universal for all future wives.
evidence.quote: a longing which shall never perish from the earth, but shall have place in the heart of every wife that loves, until the end of time
